record.title: Google social login auto-links by email without anti-pre-hijacking: pre-registered account stays accessible to attacker after victim's Google login
record.description: SocialLoginQuery resolves the account purely by email__iexact and, for an existing user, issues a session and sets email_verified=True — but never invalidates the password the account already had. Registration does not require email verification, so an attacker can pre-register a victim's email with their own password (and their own unique phone). When the real mailbox owner later uses 'Login with Google', Google proves email ownership and the backend logs them into the ATTACKER-CREATED account — while the attacker's password remains fully usable. Both parties hold persistent sessions for the same account: the attacker retains silent read/write access to everything the victim does (profile PII, store claim now unblocked because email_verified is set True, billing data). The sibling buyer-side implementation (google_customer_login) documents and fixes exactly this threat as 'Anti-pre-hijacking' by calling set_unusable_password() and sealing tokens_valid_after; the platform-users domain never received the port.
record.root_cause: SocialLoginQuery (services/social.py:103-147) performs find-or-create by verified provider email but, on the existing-account branch, only fills email_verified/names — it does not check whether the matched account's email was ever verified, does not invalidate a usable password, and does not revoke outstanding sessions. The credential proof covers the EMAIL, not the party who chose the existing password.
record.intended_behavior: Mirror the customer-side contract (StoreApp/domains/customers/services/google.py:153-165): when Google proves ownership of an email that matches a pre-existing account, any usable password must be invalidated and prior sessions sealed, so only the mailbox owner (via Google or password-reset) retains access.

trace.description: POST /api/auth/google/ {credential} → VerifyGoogleCredentialQuery + SocialLoginQuery → _social_session_response issues the DAVENT session
user = User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).first() — matches ANY account with that email, including one pre-registered by an attacker with unverified email and a usable password
existing-account branch sets profile.email_verified=True and names only — no has_usable_password check, no set_unusable_password, no session revocation, no prior-verification gate
RefreshToken.for_user(user) mints refresh+access for the Google-verified caller while the pre-registrant's password still authenticates via POST /api/token/

evidence.description: Account resolution is email-only; no link between the Google identity (sub) and the account — pure auto-link by email
Existing-account branch (lines 134-147) only updates email_verified/names; zero hardening on credentials or sessions
RegisterUserQuery uses create_user(password=...) leaving a usable password and email_verified=False; verification mail is async and not required for account use
Sibling anti-pre-hijacking block: 'Google probó la titularidad del EMAIL, no quién eligió la contraseña' → set_unusable_password() + tokens_valid_after seal (lines 160-165)
phone_hash unique=True — one account per phone limits the attack to targeted pre-registration
test_google_links_existing_user_by_email codifies the unguarded auto-link (200 + email_verified=True, password untouched)
_revoke_sessions exists (bulk-blacklists all OutstandingToken) but SocialLoginQuery never calls it

conditions.description: Attacker needs only anonymous access: POST /api/register/ is open (IsAnonimous) and POST /api/token/ requires only the chosen password.
The victim's email must be unregistered when the attacker pre-registers it, and the victim must later authenticate with Google on that same email.
GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID must be configured; otherwise GoogleAuthView returns 503 and the feature is off.
The victim must control a Google account whose verified email equals the pre-registered address.

execution.attacker_perspective: Unauthenticated internet user who knows or guesses a target's email address.
payloads: POST /api/register/ {username: 'attacker1', email: 'victim@example.com', password: 'Attacker!23', phone: '+5491100000001', accept_terms: true}
POST /api/auth/google/ {credential: '<Google ID token for victim@example.com>'}  // performed by the VICTIM
instructions: 1. Attacker registers an account via POST /api/register/ using the victim's email, the attacker's own password, and a unique phone number (phone_hash uniqueness permits one account per phone — targeted attacks only).

2. The real mailbox owner later clicks 'Login with Google' on the platform; Google proves email ownership and SocialLoginQuery auto-links them into the attacker-created account, setting email_verified=True.
3. The attacker logs in with POST /api/token/ using their own username+password — the credential was never invalidated, so the attacker keeps a fully usable session alongside the victim's.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: SocialLoginQuery's existing-account branch (social.py:134-147) performs no password invalidation or session revocation; _social_session_response returns 200 with tokens to the Google caller; the password path via TokenObtainPairSerializer→authenticate() still returns 200 for the pre-registrant on the same User row. Both parties hold persistent sessions; profile.email_verified becomes True, also unblocking the store-claim gate.

remediation.strategy: Port the customer-side anti-pre-hijacking hardening into SocialLoginQuery's existing-account branch: when the matched account has a usable password, call user.set_unusable_password() and revoke all outstanding sessions (_revoke_sessions), so only the mailbox owner retains access via Google or password reset. Optionally restrict auto-link to accounts whose email was already verified or that were social-created.

likelihood.reason: Requires a targeted pre-registration of a specific victim email before their first Google login; phone_hash uniqueness (one phone per account) prevents mass farming, and the victim must actually use Google sign-in.

impact.reason: Yields durable, silent shared access to the victim's account — profile PII, store claim unblocked via email_verified=True, billing data — until the victim changes password or resets; the sibling code proves the threat model was known.

confidence.reason: Every step verified in current source: unguarded auto-link branch, usable-password registration, absent _revoke_sessions call, and the sibling implementation documenting the identical threat and fix.

record.title: Google login issues fresh sessions for is_active=False (deactivated) platform users
record.description: The platform password path is gated by Django's authenticate() -> ModelBackend.user_can_authenticate, which rejects is_active=False. The Google path bypasses that entirely: SocialLoginQuery looks the user up by email and _social_session_response calls RefreshToken.for_user(user) with no is_active check anywhere — for_user only logs a warning for inactive users (venv tokens.py:222-225) and still mints the tokens. However, the minted session is unusable: rest_framework_simplejwt's JWTAuthentication.get_user raises AuthenticationFailed for inactive users because CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE defaults True (simplejwt settings.py:47) and DaventProject SIMPLE_JWT does not override it — so every authenticated API call with the issued access token fails. Independently, the refresh endpoint itself rejects the token: TokenRefreshSerializer.validate applies USER_AUTHENTICATION_RULE → default_user_authentication_rule returns False for inactive users → 'no_active_account'. The deactivated principal obtains a 200 login response plus cookies but zero usable API access.
record.claimed_root_cause: Missing is_active gate on the federated session-issuance path: neither SocialLoginQuery (services/social.py:85-164) nor _social_session_response (views/auth_views.py:435-460) inspects user.is_active, unlike the password path which inherits the check from django.contrib.auth.authenticate.

trace.description: POST /api/auth/google/ → SocialLoginQuery → _social_session_response for a user looked up by verified email
User.objects.filter(email__iexact=email).first() returns the user regardless of is_active; no is_active check in the whole function
RefreshToken.for_user(user) mints refresh+access for the deactivated account — tokens issued but subsequently rejected at authentication time

evidence.description: for_user only logger.warning's for inactive users — does NOT raise; tokens are minted
JWTAuthentication.get_user raises AuthenticationFailed('User is inactive') when CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE and not user.is_active — runs on EVERY authenticated request
CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE defaults True; DaventProject/settings.py:161-166 SIMPLE_JWT does not override it

TokenRefreshSerializer.validate loads the user and applies USER_AUTHENTICATION_RULE → default_user_authentication_rule (authentication.py:182-184) returns False for inactive → refresh rejected with 'no_active_account'
Sibling customer Google login explicitly re-checks customer.is_active → 403 (parity gap exists but yields no usable session here)
Full read of SocialLoginQuery confirms zero is_active references (grep across AdminApp/domains/users finds only coupon.is_active in serializers)

record.reason: Refuted by two independent library-level controls in the installed rest_framework_simplejwt: (1) JWTAuthentication.get_user enforces CHECK_USER_IS_ACTIVE=True (default, not overridden) on every request, so the issued access tokens cannot authenticate to any API endpoint; (2) TokenRefreshSerializer.validate applies USER_AUTHENTICATION_RULE, which also rejects inactive users, so the refresh cookie cannot even rotate. The missing explicit is_active check in SocialLoginQuery/_social_session_response is a real parity/UX gap (200 + minted-but-dead tokens + OutstandingToken rows instead of a clean 403, matching the sibling's explicit check), but the claimed security impact — usable sessions for a deactivated principal — is not demonstrated: the deactivated user gains no API access beyond anonymous/public endpoints.

record.title: Email-verification token is not bound to the email address: a stale link verifies a newly changed, never-proven email
record.description: EmailVerificationTokenGenerator._make_hash_value signs only user.pk + user.password + timestamp + profile.email_verified — the email address is absent. UpdateUserQuery lets an authenticated user change user.email and resets email_verified=False only when it was previously True; a verification token issued while verified=False remains valid after the change because every hash input is unchanged. VerifyEmailQuery then sets email_verified=True on the account whose email is now an address whose owner never received any link. The flag is the anti-abuse gate for claiming a public store (StoreViewSet.create, viewset.py:463-469), so the attestation 'this mailbox is ours' is forged for an arbitrary unregistered address.
record.root_cause: _make_hash_value (services/services.py:202-209) omits user.email from the signed material, so the token proves only 'this user requested verification at time T', not 'this specific address was proven'.
record.intended_behavior: email_verified must attest control of the CURRENT user.email; changing the address must invalidate outstanding verification tokens (include the email — or a hash of it — in the token value).

trace.description: PATCH /api/user/ with UserUpdateSerializer {email} → UpdateUserQuery changes user.email on the authenticated, self-scoped account
email change resets profile.email_verified only when it was True; previously issued verification tokens are not invalidated
signed material = f'{user.pk}{user.password}{timestamp}{verified}' — user.email absent, so a token issued while verified=False stays valid after the address changes
check_token passes on unchanged hash inputs → profile.email_verified=True is set for an address whose owner never received a link

evidence.description: _make_hash_value returns pk+password+timestamp+verified — no email binding; comment explicitly excludes last_login but never considers email
UpdateUserQuery resets email_verified only inside `if profile.email_verified:` — when already False nothing changes and old tokens survive
UserUpdateSerializer fields=['email'] only; reachable via UserViewSet update (viewset_config.py:36-41, IsAuthenticated, queryset filtered to request.user)
validate_email only enforces iexact uniqueness against other accounts — any unregistered address is accepted
EmailVerificationTokenGenerator.timeout = 86400 (24h window)
StoreViewSet.create requires profile.email_verified (and phone) — the forged flag satisfies the anti-abuse gate

conditions.description: Any registered user with a valid access token (open registration).
Target email must not already be registered to another account (validate_email uniqueness); profile.email_verified must be False when the token is issued and remain False through the email change.
The email change plus token use must occur within the 24h EmailVerificationTokenGenerator.timeout window.

execution.attacker_perspective: Authenticated platform user wanting to forge the verified-email attestation for an address they do not control.
payloads: POST /api/register/ {username, email: 'attacker@mail.com', password, phone: '+5491100000002', accept_terms: true}
instructions: 1. Register an account with an email the attacker controls; the verification email delivers token T (uid+token) while profile.email_verified=False.
2. PATCH /api/user/ changing email to victim@example.com — UpdateUserQuery sets user.email and leaves email_verified False (it was already False, so the reset branch does not even run).
3. GET /api/verify-email/?uid=<uid>&token=T — check_token recomputes the identical hash (pk, password, timestamp, verified all unchanged) and VerifyEmailQuery sets email_verified=True.
4. The account now carries victim@example.com with email_verified=True — an attestation the mailbox owner never made; store creation's email gate is satisfied (phone anchor still required).
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: _make_hash_value omits user.email so the pre-change token validates post-change; VerifyEmailQuery sets the flag unconditionally on check_token success; StoreViewSet.create then treats the unproven address as verified for the claim gate.

remediation.strategy: Bind the verification token to the address it was issued for: include user.email (or an HMAC of it) in EmailVerificationTokenGenerator._make_hash_value so any email change invalidates outstanding links; alternatively persist the address the mail was sent to and compare it at verification time.

code_changes.fixed_code:
def _make_hash_value(self, user, timestamp):
        profile     =   getattr(user, 'profile', None)
        verified    =   getattr(profile, 'email_verified', False)
        #El correo ENTRA en el hash: cambiar user.email invalida los links ya
        #emitidos — email_verified debe atestiguar la dirección ACTUAL, no una
        #probada antes del cambio.
        return f'{user.pk}{user.password}{user.email}{timestamp}{verified}'

likelihood.reason: Trivially executable by any registered user within the 24h window; requires only reading one's own verification mail and two API calls.

impact.reason: Forges the email_verified attestation for an unproven address — defeats the store-claim anti-abuse email gate (phone anchor still required) and points account mail at an address the owner never authorized; no direct data exposure or account takeover.

confidence.reason: Hash inputs, email-change path, serializer reachability, token timeout, and the store-claim consumer were all verified line-by-line in current source; the attack sequence is fully deterministic.

record.title: No Origin/Referer check on platform session-issuing endpoints -> login CSRF (session donation) on /api/token/ and /api/auth/google/
record.description: CustomTokenObtainPairView and GoogleAuthView plant the session cookies (davent_refresh httpOnly + davent_csrf) in the response with no validation of the request Origin/Referer and no pre-session anti-CSRF token. DRF APIViews are csrf_exempt (rest_framework/views.py:149), the endpoints accept application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies (a plain cross-site HTML form POST parses into request.data), and SameSite=Lax does not prevent a top-level navigation POST response from storing Set-Cookie. An attacker auto-submitting a form with THEIR credentials (password, or a Google credential minted with the public client_id from /api/config/) leaves the victim's browser holding the attacker's refresh+CSRF cookies; the SPA's silent refresh then logs the victim into the attacker's account, and everything the victim subsequently enters (billing PII, store content) is visible to the attacker. The buyer-side auth implements exactly this defense — _session_origin_allowed is invoked on register/login/google — but it was never ported to the platform auth views.
record.root_cause: Missing origin binding on cookie-session issuance: neither CustomTokenObtainPairView.post (auth_views.py:232) nor GoogleAuthView.post/_social_session_response (auth_views.py:435-460,529-538) checks Origin/Referer against the request host or trusted origins, unlike the sibling customer endpoints.
record.intended_behavior: Session-issuing endpoints must reject cross-site POSTs (Origin/Referer allowlist = request host + CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS + CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS), matching _session_origin_allowed semantics used for customer auth.

trace.description: POST /api/token/ → CustomTokenObtainPairView; POST /api/auth/google/ → GoogleAuthView (:130) — both issue the cookie session
post() performs lockout+auth and sets cookies — no Origin/Referer validation anywhere in AdminApp auth (grep for Origin/Referer/Sec-Fetch across the domain returns only unrelated comments)

_set_refresh_cookie/_set_csrf_cookie (also auth_views.py:458-459 for Google) store the attacker's session in the victim's browser; SPA silent refresh (frontend/src/api/http.js:163-167) then authenticates as the attacker

evidence.description: Cookies set unconditionally on 200 — no origin gate precedes credential processing or cookie issuance
_require_csrf double-submit guards only refresh/logout, not session issuance
_session_origin_allowed implements the missing defense ('Anti login-CSRF … Set-Cookie aplica igual aunque SameSite=Lax') and is invoked at :232, :260, :532
APIView.as_view returns csrf_exempt(view) — Django CsrfViewMiddleware (settings.py:253) does not apply; JWT auth means no Django session CSRF either
hasSessionCookie() keys on the JS-readable davent_csrf hint; refreshCall (:163-167) posts /token/refresh/ withCredentials + X-CSRFToken — the planted cookie pair satisfies the double-submit
Cookies are SameSite=Lax — governs sending, not setting; a top-level navigation POST response still stores them as first-party cookies

conditions.description: Victim must visit an attacker-controlled page that auto-submits a cross-site form POST, then use the SPA while unknowingly logged into the attacker's account.
API and SPA must share the registrable domain (path-alias or same-origin deploy — both the compose/nginx and Render/whitenoise modes serve them same-origin) so the planted cookies are first-party.
Attacker needs a valid platform account (open registration) whose credentials are embedded in the auto-submitted form.

execution.attacker_perspective: Authenticated platform user aiming to make victims unknowingly operate inside the attacker's account.
payloads: equivalent for POST /api/auth/google/ {credential: <attacker's Google ID token minted with the public client_id from GET /api/config/>}
instructions: 1. Host a page with <form method='POST' action='https://<platform>/api/token/'> auto-submitting the attacker's username/password.

2. Victim visits the page; the top-level navigation POST returns 200 JSON and Set-Cookie stores davent_refresh (httpOnly, Path=/api/token/) + davent_csrf (Path=/) as first-party cookies — SameSite=Lax does not block setting.

3. Victim later opens the SPA; hasSessionCookie() sees davent_csrf and refreshCall posts /api/token/refresh/ with X-CSRFToken — the double-submit pair matches, rotation succeeds, and the SPA holds the attacker's access token.
4. Everything the victim enters (billing PII, store content) lands in the attacker's account.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: no Origin/Referer check exists on either session-issuing endpoint; DRF APIView is csrf_exempt; FormParser accepts urlencoded bodies; cookies are set unconditionally on 200; the frontend's silent-refresh chain consumes exactly those cookies and the planted CSRF pair passes _require_csrf.

remediation.strategy: Port the sibling _session_origin_allowed check into every session-issuing endpoint (CustomTokenObtainPairView.post and GoogleAuthView.post) before credentials are processed and cookies set; allow only request-host, CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS and CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS origins, permitting absent Origin for non-browser clients.

code_changes.fixed_code:
from urllib.parse import urlparse

def _session_origin_allowed(request):
    """Anti login-CSRF (paridad con StoreApp customers auth_views): los
    endpoints que EMITEN sesión por cookie solo aceptan POST desde orígenes
    confiables — SameSite=Lax no impide que el Set-Cookie del response de
    una navegación top-level cross-site quede guardado."""
    origin  =   (request.headers.get('Origin') or '').strip()
    if not origin:
        referer =   (request.headers.get('Referer') or '').strip()
        if referer:
            parsed  =   urlparse(referer)
            origin  =   f'{parsed.scheme}://{parsed.netloc}' if parsed.netloc else ''
    if not origin:
        return True
    host    =   (urlparse(origin).netloc or '').lower()
    if not host:
        return False
    if host == (request.get_host() or '').lower():
        return True
    trusted =   set()
    for o in list(getattr(settings, 'CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS', []) or []) + list(getattr(settings, 'CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS', []) or []):
        trusted.add((urlparse(o).netloc or o).lower())
    return host in trusted

# En CustomTokenObtainPairView.post y GoogleAuthView.post, primera línea:
#     if not _session_origin_allowed(request):
#         raise PermissionDenied('Origen no permitido.')

likelihood.reason: Requires victim interaction (visiting an attacker page then using the SPA) but no technical barrier — a single auto-submitted form suffices; classic login-CSRF preconditions.

impact.reason: Victim unknowingly uses the attacker's account — data they enter (billing PII, store content) is exposed to the attacker; no takeover of the victim's own account and no direct credential theft.

confidence.reason: All source elements verified: absent origin check, csrf_exempt APIView, form parsing, unconditional cookie issuance, frontend silent-refresh consumption, and the sibling implementation proving the intended control; browser cookie semantics are spec-defined.

record.title: AnonRateThrottle subclasses skip authenticated users -> authenticated attacker gets unbounded password-reset emails (mail bombing / SMTP+queue abuse)
record.description: Every auth-endpoint throttle in AdminApp/domains/users/views/auth_views.py subclasses plain rest_framework AnonRateThrottle (LoginRateThrottle, RefreshRateThrottle, PasswordResetRateThrottle, PasswordResetConfirmRateThrottle, SocialAuthRateThrottle, PublicConfigRateThrottle). DRF's AnonRateThrottle.get_cache_key returns None when request.user.is_authenticated — and JWTAuthentication populates request.user on every request before check_throttles regardless of the view's AllowAny permission. Any registered user (open registration) therefore bypasses ALL these IP buckets entirely. The highest-impact instance is PasswordResetRequestView: each POST /api/password-reset/ for an existing email enqueues send_password_reset_email → a real SMTP send per request, with no per-user or per-email cap — unlimited mail-bombing of arbitrary victims through DAVENT's sender identity plus Celery/SMTP queue flooding that can delay transactional mail (invoices, verifications). The buyer-side code explicitly avoids AnonRateThrottle for exactly this reason ('NO se usa AnonRateThrottle porque saltaria la cuota a un comprador autenticado', customers auth_views.py:164-168) using a customer.pk-or-IP keyed throttle instead.
record.root_cause: Throttle classes chosen as AnonRateThrottle subclasses inherit the authenticated-skip semantics; no fallback per-user throttle exists on the AllowAny auth endpoints.
record.intended_behavior: Auth endpoints that emit side effects (emails, provider calls, token issuance) must be rate-limited for BOTH anonymous and authenticated principals — e.g., a SimpleRateThrottle keyed by user.pk when authenticated else IP, as the customer domain does.

trace.description: AllowAny POST /api/password-reset/ with throttle_classes=[PasswordResetRateThrottle] — the only rate control on a side-effect endpoint

AnonRateThrottle subclass: DRF get_cache_key returns None for request.user.is_authenticated → allow_request always True for any valid-JWT caller (JWTAuthentication populates request.user before check_throttles)
existing email → send_password_reset_email.delay → SendPasswordResetEmailQuery sends one real SMTP message per accepted request, unbounded for authenticated callers

evidence.description: All auth throttles (Login/Refresh/PasswordReset/PasswordResetConfirm/SocialAuth/PublicConfig/Register in viewset.py:17) are AnonRateThrottle subclasses; only VerifyEmail/Logout use UserRateThrottle
AnonRateThrottle.get_cache_key returns None when request.user.is_authenticated; allow_request (:119-121) returns True when key is None
DEFAULT_AUTHENTICATION_CLASSES = JWTAuthentication → request.user populated pre-throttle on AllowAny views; view-level throttle_classes override the Resilient* defaults (:75-78)
CustomerRateThrottle keyed by customer.pk-or-IP with explicit comment 'NO se usa AnonRateThrottle porque saltaria la cuota a un comprador autenticado' — the intended pattern never ported

RequestPasswordResetQuery enqueues send_password_reset_email for existing emails; tasks.py:36-42 → SendPasswordResetEmailQuery performs a real SMTP send; generic 200 prevents enumeration but not volume
AdminLoginRateLimitMiddleware guards only Django admin login/password_reset paths — /api/password-reset/ has no other control

conditions.description: Any registered platform user with a valid access token (open registration).
Target email must belong to an existing account for the mail to be sent; the generic response lets the attacker spray arbitrary addresses blindly.
In production Celery is async: each accepted request enqueues a task that performs a real SMTP send; queue flooding can delay transactional mail (invoices, verifications).

execution.attacker_perspective: Registered user (free signup) holding a Bearer access token.
payloads: same pattern against /api/token/ (LoginRateThrottle also bypassed — the per-account+IP lockout still bounds credential guessing), /api/auth/google/, /api/token/refresh/
instructions: 1. Register one account and obtain an access token via POST /api/token/.
2. Loop POST /api/password-reset/ with the victim's email and the Bearer token — no 429 regardless of volume because AnonRateThrottle.get_cache_key returns None for authenticated request.user.

3. Each request for an existing email enqueues send_password_reset_email → one real SMTP send to the victim; repeat unboundedly to mail-bomb the victim through DAVENT's sender identity and flood the Celery/SMTP queue.
execution.observed_result: Source-traced: throttle key is None → allow_request returns True for every authenticated request; RequestPasswordResetQuery enqueues a mail task per existing-email request; no per-user or per-email cap exists anywhere in the chain.

remediation.strategy: Replace the AnonRateThrottle subclasses on side-effect auth endpoints with a throttle keyed by user.pk when authenticated else IP (port the CustomerRateThrottle pattern); add a per-target-email cap for password-reset requests.

likelihood.reason: Trivially exploitable by any registrant with a token; no special access, timing, or victim cooperation needed.

impact.reason: Email abuse under DAVENT's sender identity (reputation/deliverability harm), victim mailbox flooding, and Celery/SMTP queue pressure that can delay transactional mail; no data exposure or account compromise.

confidence.reason: DRF AnonRateThrottle semantics verified in the installed package, JWTAuthentication default confirmed in settings, view-level throttle_classes override confirmed, the mail-send chain traced to a real SMTP task, and the sibling implementation documents the intended pattern.
